dynamic-programming.q: Why doesn't taking the biggest coin first always work?
dynamic-programming.a: Because a choice that looks best now can rule out a better whole answer. Laaksonen's handbook gives the example: with coins {1, 3, 4} and a target of 6, greedy picks 4 + 1 + 1 (three coins), but 3 + 3 uses two. Greedy does work for some coin sets, such as the euro coins. Dynamic programming tries every coin as the last one, so it always finds the minimum.

sources.title: Laaksonen, Competitive Programmer's Handbook: greedy algorithms, the coin problem

hash-maps.q: Why can't a list be a dictionary key?
hash-maps.a: Dictionary keys must be hashable, and a list can change, so it isn't: Python raises TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'. Use a tuple instead, for example (row, col) for a grid position.

heaps.q: How do I get the largest item first with heapq?
heaps.a: heapq is a min-heap: heap[0] is always the smallest item. The classic trick is to push negated values and negate them again when you pop. From Python 3.14, heapq also has max-heap functions named with a _max suffix, such as heappush_max and heappop_max.
